OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For $n\geq 2k$ we define the deficiency of $\binom{n}{k}$ as follows. If $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime $p\leq k$ then the deficiency is undefined. Otherwise, the deficiency is the number of $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ is $k$-smooth, that is, divisible only by primes $\leq k$. 
Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$? Are there only finitely many with deficiency $>1$?
#1093: [ELS88,p.522]
number theory | 
binomial coefficients
A problem of Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS88], that was also asked in the 1986 problem session of West Coast Number Theory (as reported here).
In [ELS93] they prove that if the deficiency exists and is $\geq 1$ then $n\ll 2^k\sqrt{k}$. 
The following examples are either from [ELS88] or here. The following have deficiency $1$ (there are $58$ examples with $n\leq 10^5$):\[\binom{7}{3},\binom{13}{4},\binom{14}{4},\binom{23}{5},\binom{62}{6},\binom{94}{10},\binom{95}{10}.\]The examples which follow are the only known examples with deficiency $>1$. The following have deficiency $2$:\[\binom{44}{8},\binom{74}{10},\binom{174}{12},\binom{239}{14},\binom{5179}{27},\binom{8413}{28},\binom{8414}{28},\binom{96622}{42}.\]The following have deficiency $3$:\[\binom{46}{10},\binom{47}{10},\binom{241}{16},\binom{2105}{25},\binom{1119}{27},\binom{6459}{33}.\]The following has deficiency $4$:\[\binom{47}{11}.\]The following has deficiency $9$:\[\binom{284}{28}.\]See also [384] and [1094].
Barreto in the comments has given a positive answer to the second question, conditional on two (strong) conjectures.

 The exhaustive table of ELS93, extended from $k \le 101$ to $k \le 160$.
Prior work. Erdős–Lacampagne–Selfridge, "Estimates of the least prime factor of a binomial coefficient", Math. Comp. 61 (1993) 215–224, determined every good $\binom{N}{k}$ with positive deficiency for $k \le 101$ and all $N$, printing the results as their Tables 2 ($d > 1$) and 3 ($d = 1$). That is the computation being extended here; the reduction that makes it finite is theirs. Kevin Barreto's comments on this thread (16 Dec 2025) corrected three of the entries listed on this page and reported an $n \le 10^5$ sweep over all $k$. Nothing below supersedes either.
What is claimed. For every $2 \le k \le 160$, the complete set of $N$ with $\binom{N}{k}$ good and $d(N,k) \ge 1$ has been determined, over all $N$. Restricted to the domain ELS's tables use, this reproduces all 176 published coefficients exactly and adds six new entries, all of deficiency 1:
$k = 106$: $N = 275204387105968945551700859$
$k = 126$: $N = 36859713316079485808433663$
$k = 129$: $N = 3180883073384828665489$
$k = 136$: $N = 11665201258379042011335164$
$k = 148$: $N = 8784118930086899149724$
$k = 148$: $N = 192726492089012046660816823$
No good binomial coefficient with $d > 1$ exists for $102 \le k \le 160$ — under the tables' domain $N > k+1$, equivalently under $N \ge 2k$, the two agreeing above $k = 4$. (Without a lower bound on $N$ the statement is false for the trivial reason below: $\binom{103}{102} = 103$ is good with deficiency 101.) ELS conjectured that their list of 17 with $d > 1$ is complete; they verified it for $k \le 101$, and it now holds for $k \le 160$.
The domain, which we got wrong once. ELS state the rule for their tables as "binomial coefficients with positive deficiency for $k \le 101$ and all possible $N$", and no lower bound on $N$ is attached to the tables or to the deficiency computation other than the $N > k+1$ in their definition of $g(k)$, "the least integer $N > k+1$ such that $\binom{N}{k}$ is good". (The paper does state $N \ge 2k$ in several places — Theorems 4 and 5, Corollary 3, Case 2 — but those attach to Section 3's $f(N,k)$ and to the least-prime-factor analysis, not to the tables.) So the table criterion is $N > k+1$, which excludes only the trivial family — $\binom{k}{k} = 1$, and $\binom{k+1}{k} = k+1$ when $k+1$ is prime, which has deficiency $k-1$. (Barreto makes the same point on this thread from the other direction.) It is not $N \ge 2k$: Table 2's entry ($d=2$, $k=4$, $N=7$) has $7 < 2k = 8$, and it is the only entry anywhere in $2 \le k \le 160$ with $k+1 < N \le 2k$ — consistent with $g(k) > 2k$ for $k > 4$, which ELS quote from Ecklund–Erdős–Selfridge. Above $k = 4$ the two readings coincide, so the six new entries are the same under either, but our own earlier $N > 2k$ filter was not the table's criterion and is corrected here.
How it was checked.
1. The output is corruption-checked. Each $k$ emits a per-$k$ line whose divisor count, divisor sum and largest divisor are recomputable from $k$ alone in closed form, and every emitted row is re-derived from the definition. The whole certificate verifies in about a second (measured 0.62 s) against a roughly 30-minute production run across 10 parallel shards, about 2 core-hours in total. That detects corruption; it is not a proof of the search.
2. The enumeration was independently re-run. A second enumerator was written from the mathematical definition by a different author who had not read the first one — different divisor generation, different goodness test, different deficiency routine, no cap, no minimum-$N$ parameter. Over the full range it produced exactly the same 377 rows, with the same per-$k$ candidate and good counts. That, not the certificate, is why we believe the table is complete.
Controls that could have failed and did not: all 176 published ELS93 coefficients are reproduced exactly, in both directions, under the domain rule above; ELS's prose counts fall out of the same data (17 coefficients with $d > 1$; $d = 0$ for all good $N$ at exactly $k \in \{13,20,21,22,24,29,31,37\}$ for $3 \le k \le 42$; 11 values of $k \le 46$ with $d(g(k),k) = 1$; $d(g(k),k) = 0$ throughout $46 < k \le 149$, which ELS state they checked to 149). This check was only possible because of this thread: Barreto's $n \le 10^5$ counts are reproduced exactly, under his domain ($n \le 10^5$, $n \ge 2k$): 58 with $d = 1$, 8 with $d = 2$, 6 with $d = 3$, one each with $d = 4$ and $d = 9$. (Under the tables' $N > k+1$ the $d = 2$ count is 9 rather than 8, the extra row being the same ($k=4$, $N=7$) as above — so the domain has to be his for the comparison to be like-for-like.) His three corrections to this page ($\binom{8413}{28}$, $\binom{8414}{28}$, $\binom{96622}{42}$) are confirmed independently, and the values they replaced are absent from our table as well, as are his two additions $\binom{174}{12}$ and $\binom{239}{14}$ — present, both with $d = 2$.
His region admits $k$ up to 50000, so our $k \le 160$ table alone could not establish it. A separate reduction-free brute force over every $(n,k)$ with $4 \le n \le 10^5$ and $2 \le k \le n/2$ — no Lemma 2, goodness by Kummer digit domination — finds 74 examples in total, maximum $k$ exactly 42, and none above $k = 160$, with the same five counts. So every example in his region really does lie inside ours.
The two computations do not contain one another as specifications: his is bounded in $n$ over all $k$, this one is bounded in $k$ over all $n$, and at $k = 106$ it reaches $N \approx 2.75 \times 10^{26}$. It is only the outcomes over his region that coincide.
What is assumed. The search space is $N = a + (k-i)$ with $a \mid i\binom{k}{i}$, which is complete for positive deficiency by ELS's Lemma 2. Both enumerators use that reduction, so if Lemma 2 were false or misread, both would miss the same records and agree perfectly. It is a published theorem with a proof in ELS93, and a uniform proof of it was supplied to us during review by a reviewer (it is not ours). Independently of the reduction, a third program walks every $N$ upward and decides goodness by forming $\binom{N}{k}$ and testing $\gcd(\binom{N}{k}, k!) = 1$; run out to three times the largest $N$ the reduction can produce, it agrees exactly for $2 \le k \le 22$ and finds nothing beyond the window. Above $k = 22$ no reduction-free check was run — it is a $2^k$-sized walk — so completeness there rests on Lemma 2 as a theorem, not on a scan.
Arithmetic overflow is excluded by a bound rather than a runtime check: the accumulator only ever holds a divisor of $D_i = i\binom{k}{i}$, and $\max_i D_i + k$ first exceeds $2^{256}$ at $k = 254$, giving 93 bits of headroom at $k = 160$.
What this is not. It bears on neither headline question of [1093] — both are infinitary, and this is a finite computation at fixed $k$. It settles no case of "infinitely many with deficiency 1", and proves nothing about "only finitely many with deficiency > 1" beyond extending the range over which ELS's conjecture has been checked. The certificate does not authenticate the binary that produced it; no artifact can authenticate its own production history, and the guarantee here is the independent re-enumeration, not the provenance metadata.
Checking one entry by hand. Any one of the six is checkable on its own with a few lines of any language with big integers: form $\binom{N}{k}$, confirm $\gcd(\binom{N}{k}, k!) = 1$, then factor the $k$ consecutive integers $N-k+1, \ldots, N$ and confirm exactly one is $k$-smooth. For $k = 106$, $N - k + 47 = 275204387105968945551700800 = 2^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 13 \cdot 17 \cdot 31 \cdot 53 \cdot 61 \cdot 67 \cdot 71 \cdot 73 \cdot 83 \cdot 89 \cdot 97 \cdot 101 \cdot 103$. Full code, the certificates, both enumerators and the comparison are at github.com/bitterlemma/erdos-1093 (MIT; the README states the exact build and check commands).
Minor: read literally from $k = 2$, ELS's sentence "the only values of $k \le 42$ for which $d = 0$ for all good $N$ are 13, 20, 21, 22, 24, 29, 31, 37" omits $k = 2$, which under their own domain also has $d = 0$ for every good $N$ ($g(2) = 6$, $d(6,2) = 0$). Everything from $k = 3$ up agrees. It is possible the surrounding discussion carries an implicit $k \ge 3$.
This contribution is from the Bitter Lemma project ([email protected] — monitored; artifact requests answered). The computation, the certificate and this text were produced with Claude (Anthropic) under human direction and review; every table entry was re-verified by an independent GMP implementation that did not produce the claim.

 For $\binom{n}{k}$ with defined deficiency (i.e. $\gcd\left(\binom{n}{k},\,k!\right)=1$), we shall write $\delta(n,k)$ for its associated deficiency. This is probably useless, but I can give a resolution to the second problem under two rather strong conjectures:
$\textbf{Conjecture A}$ (Strengthening of the $xyz_{\mathrm{fin}}$-conjecture of Lagarias-Soundararajan). There exists $\kappa_0>1$ such that for all $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many primitive integer triples $X+Y=Z$ with $$\max\{p\in\mathbb{P}:p\mid XYZ\}=:S(X,Y,Z)<(\log H(X,Y,Z))^{\kappa_0-\varepsilon},$$
where $H(X,Y,Z):=\max\{|X|,\,|Y|,\,|Z|\}$.
$\textbf{Conjecture B}$ (Height forcing). Let $h_2(k)$ be the least $n\geq 2k$ such that $\binom{n}{k}$ has defined deficiency $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$. There exists $\alpha>1/\kappa_0$ such that for all sufficiently large $k$, $$h_2(k)<\infty\implies\log h_2(k)\geq ck^{\alpha}$$for some fixed $c>0$. (By PNT, we can at least show that if there is such an $\alpha>0$, then $\alpha\leq 1$).
Now, we state our result:
$\textbf{Theorem}$. Assume Conjecture A and Conjecture B. Then, there are only finitely many pairs $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 2k$ and $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ Suppose, for contradiction, that there are infinitely many such $(n,k)$. Fix one with $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$, then $\exists i,j\in\mathbb{N}$ with $i\neq j$ such that $x:= n-i$ and $y:=n-j$ are both $k$-smooth, lying in $(n-k,n]$. Set $\Delta:=\left|x-y\right|=\left|i-j\right|$, so $1\leq\Delta<k$. Since $\Delta<k$, all prime factors of $\Delta$ are $\leq k$, hence $\Delta$ is $k$-smooth. Now, consider the equation $y+\Delta=x$. Let $d:=\gcd(y,\Delta)$, and set $$A:=\frac{y}{d},\qquad B:=\frac{\Delta}{d},\qquad C:=\frac{x}{d},$$then $A+B=C$ is primitive. Because $x,y,\Delta$ are $k$-smooth and dividing by $d$ removes only primes $\leq k$, we have $S(A,B,C)\leq k$. Moreover, since $x\in(n-k,n]$, and $d\leq\Delta<k$, $$H(A,B,C)\geq C=\frac{x}{d}\geq\frac{n-k}{k}.$$Thus, $\log H\geq\log n-\mathcal{O}(\log k)$. Now, invoke Conjecture B: Since $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$, we have $\log n\gg k^{\alpha}$, hence $\log H\gg k^{\alpha}\iff k\ll(\log H)^{1/\alpha}$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ s.t. $\alpha(\kappa_0-\varepsilon)>1$ (which is possible as we have assumed $\alpha>1/\kappa_0$). Then, for all sufficiently large members of the infinite family, $$S(A,B,C)\leq k\ll(\log H)^{1/\alpha}<(\log H)^{\kappa_0-\varepsilon}.$$This produces infinitely many primitive triples violating Conjecture A, a contradiction. $\square$

 FWIW, I think, as in [ELS88], that we want $n\geq 2k$, otherwise the second question is trivial: For a prime $p$, $\binom{p}{p-1}=p$ has deficiency $p-2$, so there are infinitely many with deficiency $>1$. 
Also, the current listing of $\binom{8113}{28},\binom{8114}{28},\binom{96022}{42}$ as having deficiency $2$ seems incorrect to me. They appear to have undefined deficiency: $\binom{8113}{28}$ and $\binom{8114}{28}$ are divisible by $2,3,11,13,17,19$, and $\binom{96022}{42}$ is divisble by $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,29,41$. 
I believe the intended entries are $\binom{8413}{28}$, $\binom{8414}{28}$, and $\binom{96622}{42}$, which all appear to have deficiency $2$. Moreover, $\binom{174}{12}$ and $\binom{239}{14}$ also have deficiency $2$.
For $n\leq 10^5$, there are $58$ deficiency $1$ examples, $8$ deficiency $2$ examples, $6$ deficiency $3$ examples, and $1$ example for deficiences $4$ and $9$ each.
